routes.description: Establish that consciousness or mind is fundamental by presenting idealism as the more economical explanation of experience, information, causation, and observer-linked quantum phenomena, while supplying an account of physical development and an empirical condition that could undermine the view.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if its ontology explains experienced and physical regularities without an indispensable material substrate, connects quantum observation to consciousness without preventing pre-observer development, and identifies a publicly examinable way in which the account could fail.

motionBridge.description: Show that idealism and the cited quantum considerations jointly provide good reason to treat consciousness or a divine mind as fundamental.

centralBridges.description: Establish a cumulative inference from mental correlations, top-down causation, informational structure, and limits of material reduction to an idealist ontology.
Explain how informational evolution and observer-linked definite appearances can accommodate physical interaction and cosmic development before local conscious observers.
State empirical implications or potential defeaters that make the consciousness-dependent account publicly examinable rather than insulated from evidence.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Support the ontology by arguing that experienced properties and informational distinctions do not require an additional material substance.
Clarify what interactions and structures remain as informational evolution when no thinking observer produces definite spatiotemporal appearances.

routes.description: Require independently confirmable manifestations and mind-independent causal interaction for the affirmative claim, distinguish legitimate inference from unsupported ontology, and test whether consciousness-dependent physics explains preconscious development or instead adds an unfalsifiable divine or mental condition.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the proposed idealist and quantum inferences lack independently demonstrable support, fail to account for physical interaction and development without observer dependence, or do not yield discriminating empirical consequences sufficient to justify fundamentality.

motionBridge.description: Show that the claim of fundamental consciousness or divine mind fails the relevant public-demonstrability or physical-interaction requirements.

centralBridges.description: Establish that burden-bearing claims require detectable, repeatable, and independently confirmable consequences in shared reality.
Distinguish inferences built from mutually reinforcing demonstrable evidence from an idealist inference whose components may not independently support its ontology.
Account for forces, chemistry, and physical development through causal relations that do not depend on being mentally experienced.
Determine whether observer-dependent reality has a discriminating falsification condition and whether its additional mental commitments perform necessary explanatory work.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test the account against evolution and chemical interaction occurring before ordinary conscious observers were present.
Examine whether informational and video-game analogies entail the claimed absence of definite or maintained unobserved physical structure.

sections.title: Public Evidence and Explanatory Inference
sections.rationale: This issue sets the governing evidential burden and tests whether the affirmative cumulative inference resembles established evidence-based inference closely enough to support a fundamental ontology.

sections.title: Information, Experience, and Material Substrate
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether experienced properties, mathematics, and informational distinctions make matter explanatorily redundant or whether physical properties denote mind-independent causal capacities.

sections.title: Observer Dependence and Preconscious Development
sections.rationale: This issue is central to whether an observer-linked quantum account can accommodate evolution, chemistry, and continuing interaction before local minds without relying on an unexplained divine observer.

sections.title: Unobserved Reality and Physical Interaction
sections.rationale: This issue tests what persists without thinking minds and whether analogies involving rendering or informational evolution support the claimed relation between observation, spacetime definiteness, and causal interaction.

sections.title: Falsifiability and Ontological Parsimony
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether the consciousness-dependent account exposes itself to a discriminating empirical defeater and whether its ontological commitments satisfy the debate's demonstrability and economy requirements.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: A publicly demonstrable claim must yield detectable interactions with shared reality that different observers can independently examine, confirm, and repeat.
moves.attributionBasis: The exchange directly identifies Matt as defining his own standard of demonstrability in response to the preceding question.

response.rationale: This constructive move states the governing public-demonstrability standard, requiring shared detectable interaction, independent examination, confirmation, and repetition.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly supplies a central evidential criterion and explains how independent observers could apply it.

precisionFindings.rationale: The shared-universe assumption and the requirements of independent confirmation make the proposed demonstrability standard recoverable and bounded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The necessity claim is appropriately framed as the speaker's evidential standard after expressly setting aside hard solipsism.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from a shared universe to independently examinable sensory interaction is explicit, internally consistent, and operationally intelligible.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move provides a defensible methodological account of confirmation, though it does not independently defend repetition as necessary for every claim type.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, this directly establishes the indispensable evidential standard used by the demonstrability route.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move establishes a standard rather than interpreting a meaningful competing argument, so no live charitable alternative is tested.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly sets aside hard solipsism, assumes a shared universe, and requires demonstration to oneself and others with independent confirmation.

moves.speaker: Michael Jones
moves.proposition: Idealism is presented as an inference to the best explanation supported cumulatively by mental correlations, claimed top-down causation, quantum-cognition evidence, and the asserted failure to reduce consciousness to matter.
moves.attributionBasis: Michael explicitly compares his inferential case with acceptance of evolution and then enumerates the data he regards as supporting idealism.

components.text: Whether idealism yields detectable, repeatable consequences that independent observers can examine and confirm.

response.rationale: The cumulative inference is relevant to evidential justification but lists purported data without showing that idealism itself satisfies the preceding independent-confirmation demand.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it offers substantial contrary evidential material but leaves the decisive public-confirmation requirement uncontacted.

precisionFindings.rationale: The cumulative inference is recoverable, but quantum cognition, mental correlations, and top-down causation are grouped without stable definitions or independence qualifications.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Calling the listed considerations strong evidence for idealism exceeds the excerpt's undeveloped warrants and lack of serious comparison with rival explanations.

logicalCoherence.rationale: A cumulative inference is structurally coherent, but the bridge from heterogeneous correlations and reduction limits to idealist ontology remains materially compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt largely asserts evidential strength and nonreduction while providing no representative details, independence analysis, or comparison with physicalist rivals.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, the move directly advances the route's principal explanatory inference from the cited phenomena to idealism.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move advances its own cumulative case without expressly construing or rejecting a developed alternative interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt compares the case to inference to the best explanation and lists correlations, quantum cognition, top-down causation, and alleged nonreduction to matter.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Evolutionary inference is supported by independently demonstrable and mutually reinforcing components, including overlapping dating methods and statistical treatment of anomalies.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn begins with a direct exception to Michael's analogy and develops Matt's contrasting account of evidential support for evolution.

components.text: Whether the proposed idealist inference is evidentially analogous to accepted cumulative scientific inferences such as evolution.
Whether each component supplying the cumulative inference is independently demonstrable and mutually reinforcing.

response.rationale: The reply identifies the claimed analogy's defect: evolutionary inferences are assembled from independently demonstrable components, whereas the idealist list has not received that support.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it expressly attacks the decisive analogy and identifies the evidential consequence for the cumulative idealist inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The contrast between demonstrable components and an unsupported cumulative inference is clear, with only the generalization across scientific inference left implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move uses radiometric dating as an illustrative contrast and does not claim that one example conclusively settles the ontology.

charity.alternative: The idealist case may also be cumulative even if no single consideration independently entails idealism.
charity.decisiveQualification: Cumulative force still requires component-level support and comparative warrants connecting those components to the proposed ontology.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The diagnostic distinction is explicit and consistent: inferential conclusions gain support from independently demonstrable and mutually checking evidential components.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Radiometric dating and overlapping methods provide a concrete example, though the excerpt only compresses the promised statistical treatment of anomalies.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, the move directly supplies the comparison needed to evaluate the affirmative's inference-to-best-explanation analogy.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accepts inference as pervasive in science while fairly identifying the missing evidential difference rather than demanding direct proof of every conclusion.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes radiometric dating, demonstrable component evidence, sturdy inferential building blocks, and overlapping methods as the contrast with the idealist case.

moves.speaker: Michael Jones
moves.proposition: Because an object can be described through felt and perceived properties, Occam's razor is said to favor mental phenomena or mental information over positing an additional material substance beneath those properties.
moves.attributionBasis: Michael marks the argument as one of his main arguments and develops it through mental properties, simulation analogy, and Hume's bundle theory.

components.text: Whether the affirmative ontology is supported by independently demonstrable components rather than by an unsupported inferential bundle.
Whether mental-information ontology produces independently confirmable consequences in shared reality.

response.rationale: The parsimony argument supplies a new ontology-based consideration but does not answer either the component-demonstrability comparison or the earlier public-confirmation criterion.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it bears on explanatory economy but does not contact the decisive evidential demands of either legal target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The parsimony claim is recoverable, but mental properties, mental phenomena, mental information, and substance are not adequately distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Describing an object through experienced properties does not by itself warrant favoring an exclusively mental ontology without addressing causal or structural alternatives.

charity.alternative: A physical substrate may denote causal structure rather than an additional directly experienced bundle of qualities.
charity.decisiveQualification: A bundle description of appearances does not establish that substrate-level causal capacities are dispensable.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The argument moves too quickly from epistemic description in experiential terms to ontological redundancy, leaving a substantial category bridge unsupported.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The paper example and appeal to bundle theory illustrate the view but do not establish that mental information explains all relevant interactions.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the subsidiary tier, it strongly advances the designated parsimony bridge by arguing that an added material substance is unnecessary.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move's Occam comparison omits the strongest functional interpretation of physical substance and therefore understates the principal rival.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt describes paper through felt and seen properties, invokes Occam's razor, and asks why an additional substance is needed beyond mental phenomena or information.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Physical properties and forces describe causal interactions that need not be mentally experienced, and removing those physical components also removes the capacities by which systems interact.
moves.attributionBasis: Matt takes the invited turn and contrasts mental experience with friction, nuclear forces, molecular interaction, and water's physical effects.

components.text: Whether physical substance is explanatorily redundant once an object's perceived and felt properties have been described.
Whether removing physical components preserves the causal capacities by which objects interact.
Whether mental correlations and nonreduction make physical causal properties unnecessary.

response.rationale: The reply diagnoses that the bundle argument omits causal capacities: removing physical properties removes friction, forces, and molecular interactions, not merely an unseen label.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it directly identifies the ontology argument's missing causal function and states the consequence of removing physical components.

precisionFindings.rationale: Physical components, forces, and interaction retain a stable causal meaning, although the modal scope of mind-independent operation is implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The causal-capacity point is strong, though saying all ability to interact disappears compresses distinctions between descriptions, properties, and ontological realizers.

charity.alternative: An idealist may preserve every causal relation as informational or phenomenal structure without material substance.
charity.decisiveQualification: Renaming causal structure as information does not show that the relevant interaction capacities are dispensable or exclusively mental.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The reasoning clearly distinguishes experienced qualities from causal capacities and consistently explains why the latter matter to interaction.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Friction, nuclear forces, molecular interaction, and water provide specific representative support, though the ontological inference remains somewhat compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, the move directly advances the indispensable account of mind-independent causation and physical interaction.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly focuses on causal work rather than denying experienced properties, with only the idealist re-description left briefly developed.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that removing physical components removes interaction capacities and names friction, nuclear forces, molecular interaction, and water's effects.

moves.speaker: Michael Jones
moves.proposition: If idealism is true, the informational distinctions described by physics can refer to qualitatively discernible phenomenal states—including qualia, sensations, thoughts, and mathematics—rather than material arrangements.
moves.attributionBasis: Michael endorses the physical description, then explicitly defines information by contrasting its referent under materialism with its referent under idealism.

components.text: Whether the informational distinctions used in physical descriptions require material arrangements rather than phenomenal states.
How phenomenal information supplies the causal capacities exemplified by forces and molecular interaction.
Whether the phenomenal interpretation of information has independent demonstrable support.

response.rationale: The move contacts the substrate question by offering phenomenal states as information's referents, but it does not explain the causal interaction capacities emphasized by the objection.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the ontology component directly but leaves the decisive causal-grounding component substantially unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The materialist and idealist conditionals are explicit, but information shifts between Shannon distinctions, phenomenal states, thoughts, and mathematics.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conditional formulation appropriately states what information would refer to if idealism were true rather than claiming the definition proves idealism.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional distinction is intelligible, but it does not bridge from qualitatively discernible phenomenal states to the causal organization described by physics.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The appeal to Shannon supplies terminology, but the excerpt offers little support for treating mathematics, thoughts, and qualia as physical information's ontological referents.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly contests the asserted need for material arrangements, though it only partially addresses causal grounding.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move conditionally defines its preferred ontology but does not materially interpret or reject a developed alternative argument.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts information as material arrangements under materialism with information as qualitatively discernible phenomenal states under idealism or dualism.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: If physical development is contingent on a mind, evolution and chemical interaction before ordinary observers cannot proceed unless a divine mind is added to sustain or collapse reality.
moves.attributionBasis: Matt explicitly traces the consequences of Michael's view from mind-contingent information to evolution, chemistry, and the introduction of a divine mind.

components.text: Whether mind-contingent phenomenal information can accommodate evolution and chemical interaction before ordinary conscious observers existed.
Whether adding a divine mind is required to sustain or collapse pre-observer physical development.
Whether positing a divine mind preserves the claimed ontological parsimony.

response.rationale: The reply identifies the consequence of making information mind-contingent: preconscious evolution and chemistry require an additional observer, which pressures both physical adequacy and parsimony.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it explicitly derives the pre-observer difficulty and names the divine-mind addition allegedly needed to avoid it.

precisionFindings.rationale: The challenge is recoverable, but mind, observer, information contingency, and collapse are treated as equivalent without fully stating the affirmative's conditions.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The dilemma is powerful against continuous observer dependence, but saying evolution cannot occur assumes the view excludes uncollapsed informational evolution.

charity.alternative: Idealism could permit law-governed informational evolution before any local conscious observer encounters definite appearances.
charity.decisiveQualification: The account must still explain what evolves, how interaction occurs, and why a divine observer is unnecessary rather than merely asserted.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional objection is coherent, but its necessity claim depends on an insufficiently defended premise that all development requires contemporaneous collapse.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Evolution and chemical interaction are concrete test cases, though the excerpt does not establish that the affirmative denies deterministic pre-observer evolution.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central attack tier, the objection directly pressures the affirmative's indispensable account of physical development before observers.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection isolates a serious consequence but initially states the no-evolution conclusion more categorically than the strongest informational-evolution alternative permits.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that mind-contingent information would block evolution and chemical interaction without a mind, motivating the addition of a divine collapsing observer.

moves.speaker: Michael Jones
moves.proposition: A divine mind need not continuously watch developing events because information in the wave function can evolve deterministically until contact with a conscious observer yields a definite physical appearance through collapse.
moves.attributionBasis: Michael directly answers the challenge, distinguishes deterministic wave-function evolution from observer-induced collapse, and illustrates the distinction with a game analogy.

components.text: How evolution and chemical development can proceed before ordinary conscious observers without continuous observation by a divine mind.
Whether information can evolve and interact before collapse into definite physical appearance.
How an uncollapsed wave function grounds specific forces and chemical causal interactions.

response.rationale: The reply directly distinguishes deterministic wave-function evolution from later observer-linked definite appearance, answering the stoppage premise while leaving detailed causal interaction underexplained.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive pre-observer-development demand but does not fully explain chemical interaction or justify consciousness-caused collapse.

precisionFindings.rationale: The evolution-versus-collapse distinction is clear, but observer, physical appearance, information, and deterministic evolution lack stable scope across the analogy and ontology.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim that conscious contact causes collapse and merely produces physical appearance is asserted more strongly than the cited contextuality language warrants.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Separating deterministic evolution from definite appearance answers one premise, but the bridge from formal wave-function evolution to actual pre-observer development remains material.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The named book and wave-function description offer some support, but no defended evidence connects consciousness specifically to collapse or establishes the proposed ontology.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, this directly supplies the affirmative route's account of development before local conscious observers.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move primarily develops its own quantum account and does not depend on a substantive interpretation of a competing view.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says wave-function information evolves deterministically until contact with a conscious observer collapses it into physical appearance and invokes Quantum Enigma.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: A video-game analogy does not show that unobserved structures cease to exist, because the engine may continue maintaining the simulated environment when the player is absent or looking elsewhere.
moves.attributionBasis: Matt interrogates which observer matters and then uses the continued operation of a game engine to challenge Michael's analogy about off-screen existence.

components.text: Whether the video-game analogy supports the absence of definite or maintained unobserved structure.
Which observer is causally relevant when a game continues after the player leaves.

response.rationale: The reply diagnoses an analogy failure: a game engine may maintain and evolve its world without the player's current observation, so off-screen rendering does not establish nonexistence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it expressly probes the relevant observer and identifies why the game analogy does not entail the asserted ontological consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The counterexample is clear, though existence, maintained simulation, rendering, player, and avatar are not fully separated as technical categories.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The reply only needs the live possibility of continued engine maintenance to defeat the analogy's claimed entailment, and its questions fit that force.

charity.alternative: The analogy may concern definite rendering to an avatar rather than whether underlying computational state persists.
charity.decisiveQualification: That narrower analogy permits unobserved structure and evolution, so it cannot establish that off-screen reality simply ceases to exist.

logicalCoherence.rationale: A continuing engine is a coherent countermodel showing that observer-relative rendering does not imply absence of underlying unobserved structure.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The familiar game-engine mechanism is an apt conceptual counterexample, though the excerpt does not establish that quantum evolution works identically.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the subsidiary tier, it strongly addresses the designated limits of the video-game analogy used to characterize unobserved reality.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly distinguishes player, avatar, engine, and continued simulation while preserving the limited point that rendered appearance can be observer-relative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks which observer matters and notes that a game may keep running without the player, challenging the inference from nonrendering to nonexistence.

moves.speaker: Michael Jones
moves.proposition: Without thinking minds, interaction can persist at an informational level through deterministic wave-function evolution without objects occupying definite positions in a spacetime setting.
moves.attributionBasis: Michael answers Matt's renewed mind-removal question by distinguishing informational interaction from definite spatiotemporal physical existence.

components.text: What structure and interaction persist when no thinking observer supplies a definite spatiotemporal appearance.
Whether underlying informational evolution can persist even if definite spacetime positions do not.
How informational interaction realizes specific causal capacities and forces.

response.rationale: The reply clarifies that informational interaction and deterministic evolution persist, conceding underlying structure while denying definite spacetime position; causal realization remains unexplained.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it directly contacts persistence and interaction but does not resolve the engine-style counterexample or specify the informational causal mechanism.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between informational interaction and definite spacetime position is recoverable, but information setting and physical existence remain underdefined.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The absence of a need for definite position is treated as reason to deny it, which overstates what explanatory economy alone establishes.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The account is internally intelligible, but it infers nonexistence in spacetime from alleged lack of need and leaves informational interaction unexplained.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The assertion of deterministic wave-function interaction supplies no representative empirical support or warrant for denying definite unobserved positions.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the subsidiary tier, it directly clarifies the affirmative counterfactual concerning what remains without thinking observers.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move gives a direct account of its own counterfactual ontology rather than materially characterizing an opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that interaction persists in an information setting while definite spacetime position is unnecessary and the wave function evolves deterministically.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: The claim that physical reality would effectively stop without thinking minds is unfalsifiable and introduces unnecessary complexity under Occam's razor.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn directly follows Michael Jones's explicit confirmation and presents the opposing critique in the live dyadic exchange.

components.text: Whether denying definite physical reality without thinking minds yields a discriminating empirical falsification condition.
Whether the observer-dependent account adds unnecessary complexity under Occam's razor.
Whether deterministic unobserved evolution makes the account publicly testable rather than merely compatible with observations.

response.rationale: The reply identifies the alleged defect and consequence: if no possible observation distinguishes mind-dependent stoppage, the claim is unfalsifiable and loses its parsimony advantage.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it directly states both the testability failure and its consequence for the affirmative's appeal to Occam's razor.

precisionFindings.rationale: The objection's testability and parsimony claims are recoverable, though the exact sense in which reality stops is inherited rather than restated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker acknowledges difficulty in seeing a test, but moves from that difficulty to unfalsifiability without exhaustively excluding indirect discriminating consequences.

charity.alternative: The idealist account might be indirectly falsifiable through quantum predictions even if the no-mind condition cannot itself be observed.
charity.decisiveQualification: A genuine defeater must discriminate consciousness dependence from rival quantum interpretations rather than merely conflict with quantum mechanics generally.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The connection between untestability and reduced parsimony is coherent, with one bounded gap concerning whether indirect tests could discriminate the account.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The critique correctly identifies a missing test in the presented account, but the excerpt offers assertion rather than a systematic exclusion of possible falsifiers.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly advances the route's indispensable assessment of discriminating testability and ontological economy.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection fairly identifies the core testability problem, though its brief formulation does not itself examine every possible indirect empirical consequence.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt calls the mind-dependent proposition impossible to argue against, labels it unfalsifiable, and says it violates Occam's razor.

moves.speaker: Michael Jones
moves.proposition: The consciousness-dependent account is claimed to be falsifiable because finding hidden variables compatible with quantum mechanics would undermine its appeal to contextuality and observer-dependent perceived reality.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly answers the immediately preceding falsifiability objection and reconnects the answer to his opening quantum-mechanical argument.

components.text: Whether the consciousness-dependent account has an empirical condition whose satisfaction would undermine it.
Whether hidden variables would specifically falsify consciousness-caused collapse rather than only one contextuality argument.
Whether Kochen-Specker evidence independently supports the full idealist ontology.

response.rationale: The reply names hidden variables as a potential defeater and therefore contacts the falsifiability demand, but it does not show that this result uniquely tests consciousness dependence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it supplies a concrete proposed defeater but leaves the decisive discrimination from rival quantum interpretations unsupported.

precisionFindings.rationale: A proposed hidden-variable defeater is identifiable, but hidden variables, noncontextuality, perceived reality, and consciousness dependence are not kept coextensive.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Saying one must find hidden variables overstates the link between Kochen-Specker contextuality and the much stronger claim that consciousness is fundamental.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move offers a falsification structure, but the inference from noncontextual hidden variables to defeat of consciousness-dependent ontology is insufficiently bridged.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Naming Kochen-Specker and a confirming experiment adds specificity, yet the excerpt does not establish consciousness, collapse, or idealism as their unique implication.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, the move directly addresses the affirmative route's indispensable public-demonstrability and potential-defeater requirement.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move proposes its own empirical defeater without materially construing or weakening an opposing interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says hidden variables would falsify the account, invokes experimental confirmation of Kochen-Specker, and connects noncontextuality with perceived reality.
